derives_from: Gujarati has no published pronunciation key of the kind Bhargava's dictionary gives Hindi -- Gujarati lexicography does not print a respelling column, because the orthography is shallow enough not to need one -- so this table adapts the mechanism rather than a book. It is generated from `hi__hi-IN.json`, which follows Bhargava's page layout and the *Rapidex English Speaking Course*'s letter-for-sound choices, with every Devanagari character mapped to its Gujarati counterpart (the codepoints are Devanagari's + 0x180 exactly, and all 57 the Hindi table emits have an assigned Gujarati counterpart) and three overrides that are facts about the Gujarati script. See content/RESPELL-SYSTEMS.md and tmp/gujarati.md. The layout is the one an Indian reader has met: hyphens dividing syllables, a prime after the stressed one, ordinary Gujarati letters, a one-line legend.

deviations.rule: standard Gujarati orthography has no nukta, and U+0ABC is banned from this table outright
deviations.why: Two independent reasons and either would be enough. Gujarati simply does not write the nukta -- there is no ફ઼ or ઝ઼ in a Gujarati newspaper, where Devanagari has क़ ख़ ग़ ज़ फ़ ड़ ढ़ and Gurmukhi has ਖ਼ ਗ਼ ਜ਼ ਫ਼. And **U+0ABC followed by a subjoined ર is one of the two sequences Noto Serif Gujarati throws on in `vendor/fontkit.esm.js`**, so a `ફ઼્ર` emitted for a /fr/ onset -- France, free, refrigerator -- would crash `core/measure.js` rather than merely look foreign. What the seven become: **/z ʒ dz dˤ/ take ઝ**, a real Gujarati letter for [z] (the historical /dʒʰ/ has gone to [z] in the modern standard, and the same letter writes loan /z/ in સાઇઝ and ઝ્લોટી), so /z/ stays distinct from /dʒ/ જ -- which is better than Telugu manages -- and collides instead with /dʒʰ/, which is Gujarati's own merger rather than an approximation. **/f/ takes ફ and therefore collides with /pʰ/**, which is this table's real cost and the same one Telugu's records: Mandarin 分 and 喷 respell alike. /q x ɣ/ take ક ખ ગ, which is what Hindi's own table already does with them, and /ɽ ɽʰ/ take ડ ઢ -- Gujarati has no retroflex flap.

deviations.rule: /æ/ and /ɛː/ take the candra-e ઍ/ૅ where Hindi gives them ऐ/ै
deviations.why: **Gujarati is the only Brahmic script in this corpus with dedicated letters for both [ɛ] and [ɔ]**, and it uses them for exactly this class of word: CLDR's own Gujarati writes ન્યુઝીલૅન્ડ, આયરલૅન્ડ, સ્વિટ્ઝર્લૅન્ડ and સૅન મેરિનો, and Gujarati print writes બૅન્ક, ટૅક્સી, કૅમેરા. Hindi's ऐ is a monophthong [ɛː] and works there; Gujarati's ઐ is read as a diphthong by many speakers, which is the objection Bengali and Telugu raised against their own ai letter and paid ya-phalaka machinery to avoid. Here it costs one letter. **/ɛ/ is deliberately left on એ/ે**, so Hindi's own split between `Man મૅન` and `Net નેટ` survives; collapsing the two would lose it. ઑ/ૉ for /ɔ ɔː ɒ/ needs no override at all -- it is Hindi's ऑ/ॉ at the same codepoint offset, and હૉસ્પિટલ and ડૉક્ટર are what it is for.

deviations.rule: /ɭ/ takes ળ where Hindi gives it ल
deviations.why: Gujarati has a retroflex lateral letter of its own, so the cells that carry /ɭ/ -- Marathi's ळ, Tamil's ள, Telugu's ళ, Russian's palatalised /ɭʲ/ and this pack's own ળ -- get the right letter rather than a plain લ. /ɬ/ stays લ: Klingon's lateral fricative has no Gujarati letter, and श/ष both stay શ for Hindi's own reason, that ષ is read [ʃ] and would spell a distinction nobody pronounces.

approximations: Sounds with no Gujarati letter, and what they get. /ʔ/ and /ʕ/ are written as nothing, which is what Gujarati already does with Arabic hamza and ain (અરબ, ઇસ્લામ) and which leaves a Thai zero onset correctly bare. /ħ/ is હ. /θ ð/ are થ દ, colliding with /t̪ d/ for the dental targets, which is the documented cost. /x ɣ q/ are ખ ગ ક and /f/ is ફ, colliding with /pʰ/, because the nukta is banned -- see the deviations. /y yː ʉ/ are યૂ and /ɵ/ is યો, which is Gujarati's own reading of a front rounded vowel (મ્યુનિક, ઝ્યુરિક, યુરો). /ø œ/ are ઓ. /ɯ/ is ઉ, following the romanisation its two largest holders use -- Japanese u and Korean ㅡ -- at the cost of Turkish ı. /ɤ/ is એ. /ɲ/ is ન્ય and /ʎ/ ल्य's counterpart લ્ય. Retroflex /ʂ ʈʂ ʈʂʰ/ merge into શ ચ છ. Vietnamese's glottalised codas and its /ˀ/ are dropped with the tone they belong to, and the Chao tone letters are dropped by `policy.tone` -- 33 of the 37 tables do, because a reader shown a tone bar on a German word would read neither.
note:
**Gujarati is Devanagari without the śirorekhā, and that is why this table is the closest derived one in the corpus.** The codepoints are Devanagari's + 0x180, the script writes the virama and the conjunct the same way, and the design decision is therefore Hindi's own: a consonant letter with nothing after it already says [ə], so a cluster that forgets its virama prints a vowel the target does not have. Every consonant has three spellings and `spellSlot`'s position decides -- bare when it is first in the syllable (`after_out: ""`), virama-then-letter elsewhere in an onset, letter-then-virama in a coda -- and the nucleus is the mirror image: an independent vowel when the syllable has emitted nothing, a sign otherwise, nothing at all for the inherent vowel.

**The word-final virama strip is kept, which Telugu had to delete.** Gujarati deletes the word-final inherent vowel exactly as Devanagari does -- ઘર is [ɡʰər], and ફોન, ટિકિટ and પાસપોર્ટ all end in a bare consonant -- so this is the second table to keep that fixup and the first Brahmic one after Hindi's own to be on that side of the line.

**A Gujarati consonant carries one vowel sign**, so every nucleus rule that emits a dependent sign has a hiatus twin that emits the independent letter instead. Hindi carries that predicate by hand for four vowels and Devanagari has the identical defect on the rest; without the generalisation Vietnamese `biệt` and Ukrainian `hryvnia` stack two signs on one letter, which is a sequence the script does not have and which neither `--gaps` nor `--units` can see.

There is **no bare `ʰ` rule**, deliberately: Hindi's `ʰ` -> "" is what let ধন্যবাদ print with its aspiration silently gone, because both halves of `dʰ` were mapped. Every aspirate has a rule of its own here, with ખ ઘ છ ઝ ઠ ઢ થ ધ ફ ભ, so an aspirate this table does not know prints a raw IPA modifier and `--gaps` catches it.
